J1_line_asserts_challenged_proposition.justification: The response challenges "The problem is a k-matroid and the greedy algorithm guarantees an approximation factor of 1/(k-eps)." Line 20 contains that content - "since the problem is a k-Matroid (is this a common term?) there will be a an approximation factor $\frac{1}{k-\epsilon}$ for any $\epsilon > 0$" - but it is not put forward as an assertion: the same sentence queries its own terminology ("is this a common term?"), it is introduced by "So I figured", and it closes "I know this is not exactly a proof yet, but am I on the right way?" (line 20), i.e. a conjecture submitted to the forum for checking, immediately after line 18's "My question: Is this valid for n-Job-Scheduling (the general case). Is this the worst-case?". The response's word "guarantees" strengthens it. So the line states the proposition but its assertoric force is genuinely ambiguous, which is what UNCLEAR is for. Note also that "approximation factor 1/(k-eps)" is never defined in the source (at k=1 it exceeds 1, which no algorithm can achieve for a maximisation problem), so the proposition itself is only loosely posed.

J2_evidence_specified.justification: A complete, runnable instance: "For k=1, three jobs with exact intervals [1,3], [0,2], and [2,4] and profits 10, 9, and 9 cause the greedy algorithm to return a profit of 10 while the optimal schedule gives 18, yielding a ratio of 5/9 which is strictly worse than 1." The parameter k, the three jobs with their exact time windows, the profits, and both claimed objective values are all given; the greedy rule it applies is the source's own at line 6 ("Greedy takes a job with the biggest profit").

J3_evidence_check.justification: Exhaustive exact evaluation of exactly the supplied instance (script kept, integers and Fractions). Reading "exact interval [s,f]" in the source's own parameters (start $s_i$, deadline $f_i$, length $f_i-s_i$, single machine), the three jobs have lengths 2,2,2, so line 4's condition $max_i|j_i| \le k \cdot min_i|j_i|$ holds with k=1 exactly as the response stipulates. Greedy by biggest profit takes [1,3] (profit 10); [0,2] and [2,4] each overlap it, so greedy stops at 10. Enumerating all 8 subsets, the only compatible pair is {[0,2],[2,4]} with profit 18, so OPT = 18 and greedy/OPT = 5/9: all three numbers the response states reproduce. This refutes the line-20 guess at k=1 under every reading of "approximation factor" I can attach to it: as a guarantee greedy >= OPT/(k-eps) it fails for eps = 1/2, 1/10, 1/100 (checked); as a ratio bound OPT/greedy <= k-eps it fails since OPT/greedy = 9/5; and even under the weaker reading "factor 1/k" it fails since 5/9 < 1. The witness satisfies the source's assumptions and falsifies the conclusion.

J4_consequence_overreach.justification: The response supplies only the single candidate 0020, the claim and the counterexample. It states no consequence beyond that line - nothing about the source's own 3-job example at lines 8-16, about line 16's "Greedy gives us w while 2(w-1) is the optimal solution", or about the n-job question at line 18 - so there is no stated consequence to overreach.

notes: Two things the second reader should weigh. (1) J1 is the soft point: line 20 is phrased as a question and the target proposition is informal, so a reader could defensibly grade J1 YES (the content is there verbatim) or NO (it is a question, not an assertion); my J3 does not depend on that choice, since the instance refutes the guess under every reading of the factor. (2) k=1 makes the guessed factor 1/(k-eps) exceed 1, so any instance where greedy is not optimal refutes it; that is a weakness of the source's formulation rather than of the witness. For context only, not part of my check: the source's own example at lines 8-16 has k=2 and ratio w/(2(w-1)), which also falls below 1/(2-eps) once w is large - I did not use this in grading, since the rule is to judge only the witness the response supplied.
